column5: entering life versus Gehenna's unquenchable fire
column6: Jesus contrasts entering life, even maimed, with being cast into Gehenna's unquenchable fire; it directly joins the commentary's two outcomes of real life and fire rather than merely naming punishment.

column5: worm does not die and fire is not quenched
column6: Mark reapplies the Isaiah image within Jesus' Gehenna teaching: the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched. It supplies a Christian continuation of the deathless, unextinguished fire imagery, while the undying subject remains the worm rather than the punished person.

column5: body and soul destroyed in Gehenna
column6: Jesus distinguishes human killing of the body from God's ability to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna; this provides a concrete Christian counter-formula to the commentary's fire in which the condemned do not die.

column5: lake of fire identified as the second death
column6: The lake burning with fire and sulfur is called the second death. The identification gives the Christian fire a death-name, in pointed contrast to 87:13's non-dying condition.

column5: death as sleep without awakening
column6: A human being lies down and does not rise, not waking or being roused from sleep until the heavens are no more; Job supplies the unrecovered sleep/death image whose absence is developed in the commentary.

column5: death swallowed forever and tears wiped away
column6: God swallows up death forever and wipes tears from faces; this is a prophetic final reversal of the commentary's place where death does not provide release and true life is absent.

column5: torture refused for a better resurrection
column6: Some are tortured and refuse release in order to obtain a better resurrection; this is a direct martyr-and-tyrant counterpart to the commentary's believing magicians facing Pharaoh's violence for a more lasting outcome.

column5: departure to be with Christ is far better
column6: Paul calls departing to be with Christ "far better," an unusually explicit Christian comparative for the commentary's assertion that the afterlife is better than the near life.

column5: earthly tent and eternal heavenly house
column6: The earthly tent is contrasted with an eternal house in the heavens not made by hands; the image maps present bodily life and a durable future dwelling onto the commentary's transient/enduring division.

column5: mortality swallowed up by life
column6: Paul says that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life, a concise Christian expression of life overcoming mortality that illuminates the commentary's definition of true life as permanence.

column5: perishable body raised imperishable
column6: Resurrection is sown perishable and raised imperishable; it gives a bodily account of the enduring life set over against death in the commentary.

column5: passing from death into life
column6: The believer has passed from death into life and does not come into judgment, a compact Johannine two-destiny formulation beside 87:13's denied life in punishment.

column5: tree of life in God's paradise
column6: The conqueror is granted food from the tree of life in God's paradise; this is a final Christian counterpart to the commentary's tree of immortality and its distinction between deceptive and true permanence.

column5: waters of life and tears removed
column6: The Lamb guides the redeemed to springs of waters of life and God wipes every tear; it combines the commentary's paradise water that gives life with an eschatological relief opposite fire-torment.

column5: water of life given freely to the thirsty
column6: God gives the thirsty person water from the spring of life without payment; it is a direct final-life-water analogue to the commentary's revivifying water in paradise.

column5: fountain of life with God
column6: The psalm calls God's presence the fountain of life; it offers a Hebrew poetic precursor for the commentary's link between life, a divine source, and life-giving water.

column5: living waters flow in every season
column6: Living waters flow from Jerusalem both in summer and winter, an eschatological water image whose ongoing flow is a close counterpart to the commentary's paradise water and abiding life.

column5: God's Spirit put within the dead so they live
column6: God promises to put his spirit within the restored people so that they live; this specifies divine reanimation by a life-giving force, the positive opposite of the fire's absence of life.

column5: hope full of immortality despite apparent punishment
column6: Though the righteous seem punished in human sight, their hope is full of immortality; this late Jewish reversal of apparent death and suffering closely complements the commentary's true, enduring life.

column5: furnace of Gehenna opposite paradise of delight
column6: 4 Ezra displays the furnace of Gehenna opposite the place of rest and paradise of delight, a Jewish apocalyptic pairing that makes the commentary's fire and true-life alternatives into adjacent final scenes.

column5: this world as corridor before the world to come
column6: Avot calls this world a corridor before the world to come and urges preparation here; its spatial-temporal image closely frames the commentary's near worldly life as preparatory rather than abiding.

column5: world to come without bodily needs, righteous enjoy divine splendor
column6: The rabbinic description removes eating, drinking, and other bodily satisfactions from the world to come while the righteous enjoy divine splendor; it offers a specific Jewish construal of the commentary's true life as more than ordinary worldly vitality.

column5: eternal fire that punishes without consuming
column6: Tertullian's final-judgment account treats eternal fire as ongoing punishment rather than a fire that simply consumes its victims, a patristic counterpart to the commentary's persistent fire; the precise translation should be verified.

column5: a fixed chasm prevents passage
column6: The great chasm between the tormented rich man and Lazarus is fixed so that no one can cross; this continuation of the water-and-fire scene adds the commentary's concern with remaining in a condition without an exit.

column5: Egyptian riches set against a future reward
column6: Moses considers reproach greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looks to the reward; it separately supplies the Egypt-specific valuation of durable reward over near advantage developed in 87:16-17.

column5: sin's wage death, God's gift eternal life
column6: Paul pairs sin's wage of death with God's gift of eternal life, a moral and eschatological life/death contrast that extends the commentary's link between life, goodness, and final outcome.

column5: sowing to flesh yields corruption, Spirit yields eternal life
column6: Sowing to the flesh reaps corruption while sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life; its present choice and later harvest closely match the commentary's worldly preference and enduring consequence.

column5: earthly-minded people have destruction as their end
column6: Those whose minds are set on earthly things have destruction as their end; this makes the commentary's choice of near life into a concrete moral orientation and eschatological consequence.

column5: heavenly citizenship
column6: Believers' citizenship is in heaven, giving the alternative to the preceding earthly-minded end a communal home that resonates with the commentary's enduring hereafter.

column5: the dead know nothing and have no further reward
column6: Qohelet says the dead know nothing and no longer have reward; within its under-the-sun argument, this is a sharp Hebrew Bible counterpoint to the commentary's afterlife as the locus of true life.

column5: the living thank God
column6: Hezekiah says that the living, the living give thanks to God; it makes active grateful goodness a mark of life, supporting the commentary's claim that bare survival without benefit or good is not life in the full sense.

column5: riches do not profit on the day of wrath
column6: Riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death; the proverb joins the commentary's benefit-language to a final reckoning that defeats merely worldly acquisition.

column5: righteous path is life and has no death
column6: The path of righteousness is life and its way has no death; this ethical use of life gives a precise Hebrew counterpart to the commentary's definition of life through good.

column5: fear of God as a fountain of life
column6: The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life that turns one from death's snares; it gives an ethical-metaphorical use of life-water, distinct from the commentary's paradise-water image.

column5: shares and exclusions in the world to come
column6: The mishnah grants all Israel a share in the world to come while listing exclusions; it gives a Jewish interpretive map of who receives enduring future life, relevant to the commentary's final division without claiming the same criteria.

column5: Sheol and death in a disputed redemption formula
column6: Hosea speaks of ransoming from Sheol and redeeming from death, but the grammar and immediate judgment context make its force disputed; its later life-over-death reception remains a cautious counterpart to the commentary's final death/life contrast.
